newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai stocks in doldrums despite baht defence.
newsitem.headline: Thai stocks in doldrums despite baht defence.

text.p: Currency speculators retreated to nurse their wounds after Asian central banks fended off attacks on the Thai baht this week, but there was little sign of relief for the country's frail stock market, analysts said on Friday.

Analysts said the Thai bourse, rated the worst performer among more than 50 stock exchanges in recent months, may get a brief lift from Thailand's success in defending its currency from speculative attacks. But few expected the prolonged downtrend in stocks to bottom soon.

"We finally got some good news that the Bank of Thailand succeeded in defending the baht, but most people feel Thailand just won the battle but not the war," said Mike Stead, chief analyst at Union Securities Co Ltd.
He said Thai stocks may, at best, stage a small technical rebound in line with the baht. The composite SET Index was down 6.56 points, or 1.18 percent, to 551.31 at 0800 GMT on Friday.

At 0800 GMT, the baht was quoted at 25.800/850 to the dollar against 25.300/340 late on Thursday. The Bank of Thailand said attacks on the currency had ended following heavy intervention from Thai and other regional central banks this week.
The baht's losses earlier this week sparked a fall in the country's stocks to near eight-year lows.
The SET Index has lost 35 percent in 1996 and 33.7 percent so far this year, including a 16.6 percent setback this month.
Analysts said weak economic fundamentals, blamed for hurting market sentiment and helping fuel rumours of policy conflicts in the government this week, remained largely unchanged.

The Thai economy is projected to grow at five to six percent this year, its slowest pace in a decade. The country's troubled property sector has sharply weakened bank earnings and pushed some over-exposed finance companies to near bankruptcy.
Economist Somjai Phagaphasvivat of Thammasat University said the government was walking an economic tight-rope.

"Thailand's dilemma is it could not lower high domestic interest rates to help revive the economy and stock market because doing it now would further weaken the baht and trigger a massive capital flight," he said.
Somjai said the central bank had few options but to maintain its high interest rate and baht fixing policies until money and stock markets gained more stability.

The Bank of Thailand said on Friday that measures would be announced on Monday to help support the stock market, including a bond issue to raise funds to purchase margin loans from securities companies.
Analysts said the market's mood remained cautious and reflected lingering jitters about the economy and the disastrous first quarter earnings of most listed firms.
"We don't know if some more bad news (is) lurking around the corner," a foreign analyst said.
Stead of Union Securities said Thai energy stocks and some electronics issues stood out as the best bargains for investors still with the nerves to return to the market.
He said Electricity Generating Plc, Cogeneration Plc, and Banpu Plc enjoyed strong earnings potential and could quickly rebound from their recent steep losses tied to the bearish market.
"I am not particularly optimistic on banks and especially finance companies. Any bank rebound will be limited," he said.
The bank and finance sectors, hurt by bad loans to property developers, have tumbled 31.5 and 58.5 percent so far this year. In March, the government ordered a revamp of the finance sector.
